source.title: Broken Latents: Studying SAEs and Feature Co-occurrence in Toy Models

record.tranche_reason: The post reports toy-model results showing when SAE latents do and do not match underlying features, and argues that co-occurrence and SAE width qualify assumptions about clean feature representations.
record.gate_note: Results reported in text include qualitative descriptions of figures, but the underlying figure values are not stated. The author’s cited findings from earlier work are not included as rows. Hyperparameters and feature probabilities used to set up experiments are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: The post trains SAEs on hand-built toy data with known ground-truth features. It reports when SAE latents do and do not match those features (one-to-one versus merged or broken latents). This bears directly on V5, whether dictionary features are the model's canonical units. It does not train a toy model that learns superposition (V1). It does not study polysemantic neurons in a trained network (V2, V3), real LLM feature distribution (V4), or feature dimensionality (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Tied SAEs resist broken latents better than untied SAEs, but still break under co-occurrence when narrower than the number of true features. The authors say this is almost certainly the LLM regime. Even single-latent SAEs merge parent and child features, so Matryoshka SAEs' core assumption is not strictly true. Multi-peak histograms suggest a fix that works in toy settings but not yet on real LLM SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: This post studies SAE representations in toy settings, including feature co-occurrence, SAE width, tied versus untied weights, and an auxiliary loss. It does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with SAE width, tied versus untied weights, feature co-occurrence, whether a parent is among the high-expected-MSE features, dimensionality, and use of the auxiliary loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Broken (merged) tied-SAE latents show multiple activation-histogram peaks, while clean latents show one peak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-peaked latent activation histograms signal SAE latents that mix co-occurring features.

fits_no_version.finding: A Gemma-2-2b tied JumpReLU SAE latent ("Canada") has multiple activation peaks; the authors' fix has not worked on real LLM SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Real LLM SAE latents can show multi-peaked activations whose cause (absorption, data distribution, non-orthogonal features) is unresolved.

fits_no_version.finding: Tied SAE latents are mutually orthogonal even when broken; the authors argue tied SAEs have a built-in orthogonality bias.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tied SAEs are biased toward orthogonal latents, which makes them more resistant to absorption than untied SAEs.

record.problems: The toy settings are not mathematical proofs, and the authors explicitly note that their conclusions may not hold for all feature co-occurrence settings. The post reports qualitative descriptions of plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The proposed activation-based technique has not been made to work well on real LLM SAEs.

untested.parts: All of V1. No network is trained to learn superposition. Feature directions are hand-set, and there is no sparsity transition or geometry result.
All of V2. There are no network neurons; only SAE latent allocation is studied.
All of V3. Polysemantic neurons in networks are not studied.
All of V4. The only real-LLM content is one histogram observation.
Stability across training runs or seeds, and completeness or canonicity in real LLMs. All V5 evidence is from toy SAEs with known ground-truth features.
All of V6. All features are 1-D by construction.

record.verdict_notes: The V1 and V2 links in the record were removed. The 'superposition' experiment imposes non-orthogonal directions by hand and only tests SAE recovery. The capacity-allocation result concerns SAE latents, not network neurons. r7, r9 and r11 are the authors' own method; they are kept under V5 only as evidence that recovery depends on training choice. All results are qualitative readings of figures, with no numeric metrics or uncertainty. The record's labels were largely reassigned to V5.

versions.untested_parts: No sparsity sweep testing a transition, no regular-geometry result, and no direct comparison with the original superposition method. The superposition experiment tests a 20-feature, 19-dimension setting with feature co-occurrence.
Tests SAE latent capacity in toy settings, not polysemantic neurons in trained networks. Does not establish a general allocation rule beyond the reported configurations.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for other reasons or whether they are evidence of superposition.
Does not measure feature distribution across LLM neurons or demonstrate recovery of sparse LLM features by a dictionary.
Tests whether SAE latents match toy-model ground-truth features in selected settings; does not test stability across training runs or whether SAE features are canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

relationships.condition: Independent features (tied or untied SAE, fewer latents than features), or tied SAE with excess latents including a parent-child setup
relationships.reason: The SAEs recover the true features one-to-one: tied SAE with 8 latents (r2, r3); both SAEs with 5 latents select features 4–8 (r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: A tied SAE with 8 latents recovered the true features one-to-one, and both SAE types with 5 latents picked out features 4–8.

relationships.condition: Standard SAEs under feature co-occurrence with fewer latents than features (including single-latent, and the 19-dim superposed setup), and untied SAEs with excess latents
relationships.reason: Latents merge parent and child features, duplicate, or combine features, instead of matching true features (r1, r6, r8, r10, r12, r13).
relationships.display_finding: Latents merged parent and child features, duplicated, or combined features instead of matching the true features.

relationships.condition: Authors' auxiliary-loss (single activation peak) training scheme in toy co-occurrence setups
relationships.reason: Whether latents match true features depends on the training scheme. The fix recovers clean latents but drops the highest-MSE feature 6 when it is the parent (r7, r9, r11).
relationships.display_finding: With the auxiliary loss, latents matched the true features cleanly, but the highest-MSE feature 6 was dropped when it was the parent, so the match depended on the training scheme.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The SAE tracks some features cleanly but mixes features 5, 6, and 7; with the modified training scheme, feature 6 remains untracked (r10, r11). These outcomes qualify any claim that sparse overcomplete settings yield clean, regular overlapping directions.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Independent features with 5 latents for 20 features
reader_labels.reason: Both tied and untied SAEs select the predicted highest-expected-MSE features 4–8 (r4, r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Co-occurring features under limited SAE capacity
reader_labels.reason: Co-occurrence produces mixed latent representations rather than a simple allocation of dedicated capacity to individual features (r6, r8).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tied SAE with excess latents and independent or specified co-occurring features
reader_labels.reason: Tied SAEs recover true features in the independent excess-capacity case and in the reported four-feature parent-child case (r2, r3).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Untied SAE with excess latents, tied SAE with fewer latents under co-occurrence, and single-latent parent-child settings
reader_labels.reason: The reported SAEs form duplicate or mixed latents, and narrow SAEs merge parent and child features instead of representing a clean parent feature (r1, r6, r8, r12, r13).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Auxiliary-loss training in toy co-occurrence setups
reader_labels.reason: The auxiliary loss repairs some mixtures, but in the high-MSE-parent case it does so while omitting feature 6, and in the reduced-dimensional setting feature 6 remains untracked (r7, r9, r11).
